extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, newspaper editors/publishers, and scholars of political science/media
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical standards for running, evaluating, and understanding metropolitan newspapers: how they gather complex news, relate to readers and advertisers, and preserve independence and public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free and truthful press as necessary public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liberties (freedom of speech/press) are of fundamental importance: a free press is necessary for the discovery and circulation of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text affirms the practical value of these civil liberties and warns that when they are in jeopardy the human spirit is at risk; but it also cautions that freedom alone does not guarantee adequate public opinion about complex matters. (Quotes: 'No one can possibly overestimate the practical value of these civil liberties.'; 'civil liberty ... does not guarantee public opinion in the modern world.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the invisible world visible (professional newsgathering)
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper's duty is to report the 'invisible environment' — distant or complex matters that citizens cannot easily observe — by assembling reliable information through appropriate institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because truth about complex matters is not self-evident, the machinery for assembling such information is 'technical and expensive' and requires institutional investment and specialized reporting. The press must provide information that makes the realities of public life 'stand out sharply against self-centered opinion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in technical and institutional capacity for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality journalism requires technical, institutional, and often costly resources to gather, verify, and present complex news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasizes that political science and democracy historically assumed information would be spontaneous, but modern reporting needs specialized machinery and education to produce usable public information: 'The machinery for assembling information is technical and expensive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve the buying public (editorial alignment with audience purchasing power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are edited and published for the 'buying public' whose purchasing power determines advertiser interest; editorial choices will tend to respect the point of view of that public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation becomes valuable only when sold to advertisers; the advertiser buys the kind of circulation that reaches likely customers (generally the fairly prosperous). Thus papers will tailor content to be acceptable to the audience advertisers want to reach: 'For this buying public newspapers are edited and published, for without that support the newspaper cannot live.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Target circulation demographics that advertisers value
rubrics_metrics.description: To be economically viable for general news, a paper must build circulation among the demographic groups advertisers prefer (e.g., fairly prosperous urban households).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains that advertisers value readerships with surplus income and discretion in buying; metropolitan key papers (cities over 100,000) supply the general news that forms the basis for national press exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alienating the core buying public
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial content should not alienate those segments of readers whom advertisers most want to reach, because losing them undermines the paper's economic base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A newspaper that angers those it most needs to reach is 'a bad medium for an advertiser.' If a paper alienates its buying public it risks losing the indispensable asset of circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate loyal, constant readership to secure independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A devoted and constant body of readers is the key source of a newspaper's practical independence from advertiser pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence increases with dependable reader loyalty: 'A newspaper that can really depend upon the loyalty of its readers is as independent as a newspaper can be.' Loyal readers can counterbalance advertiser influence and can allow a paper to resist pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many advertisers and broad readership to dilute individual advertiser influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a large number of advertisers and a wide readership reduces the ability of any single advertiser to dictate content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation from publisher Adolph S. Ochs: 'the greater the number of advertisers, the less influence they are individually able to exercise with the publisher.' Thus business strategy—growing readership and advertiser base—affects editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as primary reporters for press associations and other papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Key metropolitan dailies should supply reliable general news that becomes the source material for smaller, rural, and specialized papers via press associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roughly 175 dailies in large cities form the 'press for general news' and act as local reporters for the rest of the nation's newspapers; their reporting determines the information available to other papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance news value with audience expectations for entertainment and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers commonly expect truth but also entertainment and low price; newspapers must balance substantive reporting with features that attract and retain readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes readers' reluctance to pay openly for news and their appetite for illustrations and entertainment (e.g., Sunday supplements), observing that the public will pay little directly for news but will pay for entertainment/advertised goods—so editorial strategy must reflect these economic realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and present objective measures and audits to increase public control
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring government and large institutions into meaningful public accountability, news and public institutions should develop standards of living and audits whose results can be plainly recorded and objectively measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a broader political point, the author argues that the press (and institutions) should insist that public acts be plainly recorded and their results objectively measured so citizens can progressively increase control over officials: 'Outside the rather narrow range of our own possible attention, social control depends upon devising standards of living and methods of audit...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of laissez-faire truth discovery and provide educative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must not assume that free competition of opinions alone will produce truth for complex issues; it should provide educative reporting and institutions that teach or explain the larger context to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic doctrines (Milton, Mill) that truth will win in open encounter are valuable but insufficient for complex/invisible matters; thus newspapers must go beyond mere platforming of opinions to active reporting and explanation.
